en: Thus have I heard— *Dīgha Nikāya 17, Mahāsudassanasutta*
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kusinārā in the Upavattana, the Sal-tree grove of the Mallas, between the twin Sāla trees, at the time of his final Nibbāna.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“May the Blessed One, venerable sir, not attain final Nibbāna in this insignificant little town, this dusty backwater town, this branch township.”
"Venerable sir, there are other great cities:
namely, Campā, Rājagaha, Sāvatthī, Sāketa, Kosambī, and Bārāṇasī;
let the Blessed One attain final nibbāna in one of these."
“In this place there are many wealthy khattiyas, wealthy brahmins, and wealthy householders who have deep faith in the Tathāgata; they will perform the funeral rites for the body of the Tathāgata.
“Do not say that, Ānanda! Do not say that, Ānanda:
‘It is a mere wattle-and-daub town, a backwater town, a branch township.’”
1. The Royal Capital of Kusāvatī.
Once upon a time, Ānanda, there was a consecrated kṣatriya king named Mahāsudassana, a conqueror of the four quarters who had attained stability over the realm.
For King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, this Kusinārā was the royal capital named Kusāvatī.
It was twelve yojanas in length from east to west, and seven yojanas in width from north to south.
Ānanda, the royal capital Kusāvatī was prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and well-supplied with food.
Just as, Ānanda, the royal capital of the devas named Āḷakamandā is prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with yakṣas, and well-supplied with food; so too was Kusāvatī.
In the same way, Ānanda, the royal capital Kusāvatī was prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and well-supplied with food.
The royal capital Kusāvatī, Ānanda, was never devoid of ten sounds, both by day and by night; that is to say:

the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of kettledrums, the sound of tabors, the sound of lutes, the sound of singing, the sound of conchs, the sound of cymbals, and the tenth sound: "Eat! Drink! Feast!"
Ānanda, the royal capital Kusāvatī was surrounded by seven encircling walls:
one wall was made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, one of crystal, one of ruby, one of emerald, and one of all kinds of gems.
Ānanda, the royal capital Kusāvatī had gates of four colors.
One door was made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.
At each door, seven pillars were set up, three fathoms in girth, three fathoms in depth, and twelve fathoms in height.
One pillar was made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, one of crystal, one of ruby, one of emerald, and one of all kinds of gems.
Ānanda, the royal capital Kusāvatī was surrounded by seven rows of palm trees.
One row of palms was made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, one of crystal, one of ruby, one of emerald, and one of every kind of gem.
On the golden palm tree, the trunk was made of gold, while the leaves and fruit were made of silver.
The silver palm tree had a trunk made of silver, with leaves and fruit made of gold.
The beryl palm tree had a trunk made of beryl, with leaves and fruit made of crystal.
The crystal palm tree had a trunk made of crystal, with leaves and fruit made of beryl.
The trunk of the ruby palm was made of ruby, and its leaves and fruits were made of emerald.
The trunk of the emerald palm was made of emerald, and its leaves and fruits were made of ruby.
The trunk of the all-jewel palm was made of all jewels, and its leaves and fruits were made of all jewels.
Now, Ānanda, as those rows of palm trees were stirred by the wind, their sound was lovely, enchanting, pleasing, and intoxicating.
Just as, Ānanda, the sound of a five-piece musical ensemble—well-trained, well-tuned, and skillfully performed—is lovely, enchanting, pleasing, and intoxicating;
even so, Ānanda, the sound of those rows of palm trees stirred by the wind was lovely, enchanting, pleasing, and intoxicating.

Moreover, Ānanda, those who at that time were libertines, drunkards, and gluttons in the royal capital of Kusāvatī enjoyed themselves with the sound of those rows of palm trees as they rustled in the wind.
2. Endowed with the Seven Jewels 2.1.
The Wheel-Jewel (Cakraratna)
“Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was endowed with seven treasures and four kinds of success.
With which seven?
Here, Ānanda, on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, having bathed his head and observed the Uposatha, King Mahāsudassana had gone up to the upper terrace of his magnificent palace.”
The divine wheel-treasure appeared, with its thousand spokes, its rim, and its hub, complete in every respect.
Upon seeing it, King Mahāsudassana thought:
"I have indeed heard this: 'When, for a head-anointed Khattiya king, on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth..."

‘When one who has bathed his head, observed the Uposatha, and ascended to the excellent upper palace, the divine Wheel-Treasure appears—thousand-spoked, with a rim and a hub, complete in every respect; he is a Wheel-turning Monarch.
‘Shall I indeed become such a Wheel-turning Monarch?’”

Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, took hold of the golden water-pitcher with his left hand, and sprinkled the Wheel-Treasure with his right hand, saying:
"May the noble Wheel-Treasure roll forth! May the noble Wheel-Treasure conquer!
Then, Ānanda, that Wheel-Treasure rolled toward the eastern direction, and King Mahāsudassana followed right after it.
Together with his fourfold army, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana would take up residence wherever the wheel-treasure came to a halt, together with that fourfold army.
And as for those rival kings in the eastern direction, Ānanda, they approached King Mahāsudassana and spoke thus:
"Come, Great King! Welcome to you, Great King! This is your own realm, Great King;
give your commands, Great King! King Mahāsudassana said:

"No living being is to be killed; what is not given is not to be taken; one must not engage in sexual misconduct; one must not speak falsehoods; intoxicants are not to be drunk; and you should eat only according to what has been provided."
Furthermore, Ānanda, those rival kings in the eastern direction became followers of King Mahāsudassana.
Then, Ānanda, that Wheel-Treasure, having plunged into the eastern ocean and emerged again, proceeded toward the southern direction...
[as before] ...having plunged into the southern ocean and emerged again, it proceeded toward the western direction... [as before].
Having plunged into the western ocean and emerged from it, it proceeded toward the northern direction, and King Mahāsudassana followed right after it with his fourfold army.
In whatever place, Ānanda, the Wheel-Treasure came to a halt, there King Mahāsudassana took up residence together with his fourfold army.
And as for those rival kings in the northern direction, Ānanda, they approached King Mahāsudassana and spoke thus:
"Come, Great King! Welcome to you, Great King! This is your own domain, Great King; give your commands, Great King! King Mahāsudassana replied:

"No living being is to be killed; what is not given is not to be taken; one must not engage in sexual misconduct; no falsehood is to be spoken; intoxicants are not to be drunk; and you should eat only as much as is necessary."
Furthermore, Ānanda, those rival kings in the northern direction became followers of King Mahāsudassana.
Then, Ānanda, having conquered the earth as far as the ocean,
that Wheel-Treasure returned to the royal capital of Kusāvatī and stood before the gate of King Mahāsudassana’s inner palace, at the head of the hall of justice, with its rim facing upward.
I imagine it stood there, beautifying King Mahāsudassana’s inner palace.
Such was the Wheel-Treasure, Ānanda, that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.
2.2. The Elephant-Treasure.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the elephant-treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana:
it was all-white, with sevenfold-limbed feet, possessed of supernormal power, able to travel through the air, a royal elephant named Uposatha.
Upon seeing him, King Mahāsudassana’s heart was filled with confidence:
“‘How excellent indeed, sir, is this elephant vehicle, were it to become well-tamed!
Then, Ānanda, that elephant-treasure—just as a noble scented elephant well-trained for a long time would—likewise attained a state of taming.
Once upon a time, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, while testing that very elephant-treasure, in the morning time...”
Having mounted it, he traveled across the earth bounded by the ocean, and upon returning to the royal capital of Kusāvatī, he took his morning meal.
Such, Ānanda, was the elephant-treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.
2.3. The Horse-Treasure.
Furthermore, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana’s horse-treasure appeared:
a royal steed named Valāhaka, entirely white, with a black head, a mane like muñja grass, possessed of supernormal power, able to travel through the air, and endowed with psychic might.
Upon seeing him, King Mahāsudassana’s heart was filled with serene confidence.
“It would indeed be excellent, sir, if this noble steed were to submit to training.
Then, Ānanda, that jewel of a horse, just as a noble thoroughbred horse well-trained for a long time would, likewise submitted to the training.
Once upon a time, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, desiring to test that very jewel of a horse, [set out] in the morning...
Having mounted it, he traveled across the earth as far as the ocean’s edge, and upon returning to the royal capital of Kusāvatī, he took his morning meal.
Such, Ānanda, was the horse-treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana.
2.4. The Jewel-Treasure.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the jewel-treasure appeared for King Mahāsudassana.
It was a beryl gem, beautiful, of pure origin, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear, translucent, unclouded, and perfect in every respect.
Moreover, Ānanda, the radiance of that jewel-treasure pervaded an area of one league all around.

"Once upon a time, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, desiring to test that very jewel-treasure, arrayed his fourfold army, hoisted the jewel upon the top of his banner, and set out in the thick darkness of the night.
And those villages in the vicinity, Ānanda, engaged in their work by that light, thinking it was day.
Such, Ānanda, was the jewel-treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana."
2.5. The Woman-Jewel.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the woman-jewel appeared to King Mahāsudassana;

she was beautiful, lovely, and charming, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion; she was neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too fair, surpassing the human appearance yet not having reached the divine appearance.
Moreover, Ānanda, the touch of that woman-treasure is like that of a tuft of cotton or a tuft of silk-cotton.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the limbs of that woman-treasure are warm in the cold and cool in the heat.
Moreover, Ānanda, the scent of sandalwood emanates from the body of that woman-treasure, and the scent of blue lotus from her mouth.
Now, Ānanda, that jewel of a woman rose before King Mahāsudassana and retired after him; she was attentive to his needs, acted with kindness, and spoke with affection.
Moreover, Ānanda, that jewel of a woman did not even transgress against King Mahāsudassana in thought, much less in body.
Such a jewel of a woman appeared, Ānanda, for King Mahāsudassana.
2.6. The Householder-Treasure Furthermore, Ānanda, the householder-treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana.
Born of the ripening of his kamma, he possessed a divine eye by which he could see hidden treasures, both those with an owner and those without an owner.
So he approached King Mahāsudassana and said:
“Be at ease, Your Majesty; I shall perform for you whatever needs to be done with wealth by means of wealth.
Once in the past, Ānanda, while testing that very treasurer-jewel, King Mahāsudassana boarded a boat, entered the current in the middle of the river Ganges, and said this to the treasurer-jewel:
“I have need for gold and silver, householder.
“In that case, Great King, let the ship come to one shore.
“I have need for gold and silver right here, householder.”
Then, Ānanda, that householder-treasure, having dipped both hands into the water and drawn up a jar full of gold and bullion, said this to King Mahāsudassana:
“Is this enough, Great King? Is this done enough, Great King? Is this honored enough, Great King?
King Mahāsudassana replied thus:
‘Enough of this, householder; enough of this, householder; enough has been honored, householder.
Such was the householder-treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda.
2.7. The Counsellor-Treasure.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the counselor-treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana—
wise, competent, intelligent, and capable of leading King Mahāsudassana to what should be approached, away from what should be avoided, and establishing him in what should be established.
He approached King Mahāsudassana and spoke thus:
"Be free from anxiety, Your Majesty; I shall provide guidance.
Such was the counselor-treasure that appeared to King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda.
King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, was endowed with these seven treasures.
3. Possessed of the Four Psychic Powers:
Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was possessed of four psychic powers. Which four?
In this regard, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was handsome, beautiful, and pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, far surpassing other men.
By this first supernormal power, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was endowed.
Furthermore, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was long-lived and long-enduring, far surpassing other men.
King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, was endowed with this second supernormal power.

Furthermore, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was free from illness and free from affliction; he possessed a digestive system that was perfectly balanced, being neither too cold nor too hot, and was far superior to that of other men.
King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, was endowed with this third supernormal power.
Furthermore, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was dear and pleasing to the brahmins and householders.
Just as a father is dear and pleasing to his children,
even so, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was dear and pleasing to the brahmins and householders.
The brahmins and householders were also dear and pleasing to King Mahāsudassana,
Ānanda. Just as sons are dear and pleasing to a father, even so,
Ānanda, the brahmins and householders were dear and pleasing to King Mahāsudassana.
“Once upon a time, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana set out for the pleasure gardens with his fourfold army.
Then, Ānanda, the brahmins and householders approached King Mahāsudassana and said to him:
‘Go slowly, Your Majesty, so that we may see you for longer.’”
King Mahāsudassana also, Ānanda, addressed his charioteer:
"Drive the chariot slowly, charioteer, so that I may see the brahmins and householders for longer.
King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, was endowed with this fourth supernormal power.
“Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was endowed with these four supernormal powers. 4.
The Dhamma Palace and the Lotus Pond.
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to King Mahāsudassana:”
‘What if I were to have lotus ponds constructed at intervals of one hundred bow-lengths among these palm trees?
Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana had lotus ponds constructed at those intervals of one hundred bow-lengths.
Now, Ānanda, those lotus ponds were built with bricks of four colors.
One of the bricks was made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those lotus ponds each had four staircases of four different colors:
one staircase was made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.
The golden staircase had pillars made of gold, with railings and coping made of silver.
The silver staircase had pillars made of silver, with railings and coping made of gold.
The beryl staircase had pillars made of beryl, with railings and coping made of crystal.
The steps of the staircase made of crystal had pillars made of crystal, with railings and coping stones made of beryl.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those lotus ponds were surrounded by two kinds of railings: one railing was made of gold and the other was made of silver.

On the golden railing, the pillars were made of gold, while the railings and coping stones were made of silver. On the silver railing, the pillars were made of silver, while the railings and coping stones were made of gold.
The railings were made of silver; the pillars were of silver, and the crossbars and coping stones were of gold.
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to King Mahāsudassana:
"What if I were to have such a kind of garland planted in these lotus ponds—blue water-lilies, red lotuses, white water-lilies, and white lotuses—blooming in all seasons and open to all people?"
Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana caused such lotuses—blue, red, yellow, and white—to be planted in those ponds, which were seasonal and open to all people.
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to King Mahāsudassana:
"What if I were to appoint men as bath-attendants for these ponds, who would bathe every person who comes?"
“Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana appointed men as bath-attendants on the banks of those lotus ponds, who bathed whoever came to them.
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to King Mahāsudassana:
‘What if I were to establish such a gift on the banks of these lotus ponds—’”
‘Food for one who needs food, drink for one who needs drink, clothing for one who needs clothing, a vehicle for one who needs a vehicle,
a bed for one who needs a bed, a woman for one who needs a woman, silver for one who needs silver, and gold for one who needs gold.’”
Ānanda, on the banks of those lotus ponds, King Mahāsudassana established such a gift:
food for those in need of food, drink for those in need of drink, clothing for those in need of clothing, vehicles for those in need of vehicles, bedding for those in need of bedding,
women for those in need of women, silver for those in need of silver, and gold for those in need of gold.
Then, Ānanda, the brahmins and householders, taking with them abundant wealth, approached King Mahāsudassana and said:
“Sire, this abundant wealth has been brought specifically for Your Majesty; may Your Majesty accept it.
“Enough, sirs! This abundant wealth of mine was acquired through righteous taxation; let it remain yours, and bring even more besides.”
Refused by the king, they stepped aside and reflected thus:
"It would not be fitting for us to take these possessions back to our own homes.
What if we were to build a residence for King Mahāsudassana?"
They approached King Mahāsudassana and said to him:
“We shall build a palace for you, O Lord.
King Mahāsudassana consented by remaining silent, Ānanda.
Then, Ānanda, Sakka, lord of the devas, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in King Mahāsudassana’s mind, addressed the young deva Vissakamma:
“Come, friend Vissakamma, build a dwelling for King Mahāsudassana—a palace named Dhamma.
“Very well, venerable sir,” Vissakamma, the young deva, replied to Sakka, lord of the devas.
Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, even so,
having vanished from among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, he appeared before King Mahāsudassana.
Then, Ānanda, the devaputta Vissakamma said this to King Mahāsudassana:
‘Your Majesty, I shall build for you a residence called the Palace of Dhamma.
Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana consented by remaining silent.
Ānanda, the divine son Vissakamma built for King Mahāsudassana that residence, the Palace named Dhamma.
Ānanda, the Palace of Dhamma was one league in length from east to west and half a league in width from north to south.
Ānanda, the foundation of the Palace of Dhamma was built three men high with bricks of four colors—
one brick made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.
Ānanda, the palace Dhamma had eighty-four thousand pillars of four kinds:
one pillar was made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.
Ānanda, the palace Dhamma was paved with floor-boards of four kinds.
One floor was made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.
Ānanda, the palace of Dhamma had twenty-four staircases of four colors:
one staircase was made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.
The golden staircase had pillars made of gold, with railings and coping made of silver.
The silver staircase had pillars made of silver, with railings and coping made of gold.
The beryl staircase had pillars made of beryl, with railings and coping made of crystal.
The stairs made of crystal had pillars made of crystal, and their railings and handrails were made of beryl.
In the palace Dhamma, Ānanda, there were eighty-four thousand gabled chambers of four kinds:
one chamber was made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.
In the gabled chamber made of gold, a couch made of silver was prepared; in the gabled chamber made of silver, a couch made of gold was prepared;
in the gabled chamber made of beryl, a couch made of ivory was prepared;
in the gabled chamber made of crystal, a couch made of heartwood was prepared.
At the door of the gabled chamber made of gold stood a palmyra tree made of silver; its trunk was of silver, and its leaves and fruit were of gold.
At the door of the gabled chamber made of silver stood a palmyra tree made of gold; its trunk was of gold, and its leaves and fruit were of silver.
At the door of the gabled chamber made of beryl stood a palmyra tree made of crystal; its trunk was of crystal, and its leaves and fruit were of beryl.
At the door of the gabled chamber made of crystal stood a palmyra tree made of beryl; its trunk was made of beryl, and its leaves and fruit were made of crystal.
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to King Mahāsudassana:
"What if I were to have a grove of palmyra trees made entirely of gold established at the door of the Great Gabled Chamber, where I might sit for my midday rest?"
Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana had a palm grove made entirely of gold at the entrance to the Great Gabled Hall, where he would sit for his midday rest.
Ānanda, the Palace of Dhamma was surrounded by two railings: one railing was made of gold and the other of silver.

On the golden railing, the pillars were made of gold, while the crossbars and the finials were made of silver. On the silver railing, the pillars were made of silver, while the crossbars and the finials were made of gold.
The silver railing had pillars made of silver, with gold pins and finials.
The Palace of Dhamma, Ānanda, was surrounded by two networks of tinkling bells—
one network made of gold and one made of silver.
The golden lattice had silver bells, and the silver lattice had golden bells.
Now, Ānanda, when those lattices of bells were stirred by the wind, their sound was lovely, enchanting, pleasing, and intoxicating.

Just as, Ānanda, the sound of a five-piece musical ensemble—well-trained, well-tuned, and performed with great skill—is lovely, enchanting, pleasing, and intoxicating; so too was the sound of those lattices of bells.
In the same way, Ānanda, when those networks of bells were stirred by the wind, their sound was lovely, enchanting, pleasing, and intoxicating.
And at that time, Ānanda, those who were libertines, drunkards, and gluttons in the royal capital of Kusāvatī took their pleasure by means of the sound of those networks of bells stirred by the wind.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the Dhamma Palace, once completed, was difficult to look upon; it dazzled the eyes.

"Just as, Ānanda, in the last month of the rains, during the autumn season, when the sky is clear and free of clouds, the sun as it rises in the heavens is difficult to look upon and dazzles the eyes;
even so, Ānanda, the Palace of Dhamma was difficult to look upon and dazzled the eyes.
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to King Mahāsudassana:"
‘What if I were to have a lotus pond named Dhamma constructed in front of the Palace of Dhamma?
Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana had a lotus pond named Dhamma constructed in front of the Palace of Dhamma.
Ānanda, the Dhamma lotus pond was one *yojana* in length from east to west, and half a *yojana* in width from north to south.
Ānanda, the Dhamma lotus pond was built with bricks of four colors:
one brick was made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.
Ānanda, the Dhamma lotus pond had twenty-four stairways of four colors.
One staircase was made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl, and one of crystal.
On the golden staircase, the pillars were of gold, while the crossbars and the handrails were of silver.
On the silver staircase, the pillars were of silver, while the crossbars and the handrails were of gold.
The steps of the staircase made of beryl had pillars made of beryl, with railings and handrails made of crystal.
The steps of the staircase made of crystal had pillars made of crystal, with railings and handrails made of beryl.
Ānanda, the lotus pond Dhammā was surrounded by two kinds of railings: one railing was made of gold, and the other was made of silver.
In the golden railing, the pillars were made of gold, while the crossbars and the coping were made of silver.
In the silver railing, the pillars were made of silver, while the crossbars and the coping were made of gold.
Ānanda, the Dhamma lotus pond was surrounded by seven rows of palm trees.
There was one row of palm trees made of gold, one made of silver, one made of beryl, one made of crystal, one made of ruby, one made of emerald, and one made of all kinds of gems.
The golden palm tree had a trunk of gold, with leaves and fruit made of silver.
The silver palm tree had a trunk of silver, with leaves and fruit made of gold.
The beryl palm tree had a trunk made of beryl, with leaves and fruit made of crystal.
The crystal palm tree had a trunk made of crystal, with leaves and fruit made of beryl.
The ruby palm tree had a trunk made of ruby, with leaves and fruit made of masāragalla stone.
The trunk of the palm tree made of masāragalla stone was of masāragalla stone, and its leaves and fruits were of ruby (lohitaṅka).
The trunk of the palm tree made of every kind of jewel was of every kind of jewel, and its leaves and fruits were of every kind of jewel.
Now, Ānanda, when those rows of palm trees were stirred by the wind, their sound was lovely, enchanting, pleasant, and intoxicating.
"Just as, Ānanda, the sound of a five-piece musical ensemble—well-trained, well-tuned, and skillfully performed—is lovely, enchanting, pleasing, and intoxicating;
even so, Ānanda, the sound of those rows of palm trees stirred by the wind was lovely, enchanting, pleasing, and intoxicating."

Furthermore, Ānanda, those who at that time were libertines, drunkards, and gluttons in the royal capital of Kusāvatī enjoyed themselves with the sound of those rows of palm trees as they rustled in the wind.
And when, Ānanda, the Palace of Dhamma was finished and the Dhamma lotus pond was completed,
King Mahāsudassana [invited] those who at that time were regarded as ascetics among ascetics or regarded as brahmins among brahmins, and he [provided for them] with all their desires.
Having satisfied them, he ascended the Dhamma Palace.
First Recitation Section.
5. Attainment of Jhāna.
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to King Mahāsudassana:
"Of what deed is this the fruit, of what deed is this the ripening, that I am now so powerful and so majestic?
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to King Mahāsudassana:
“This is the fruit of three kinds of action, the result of three kinds of action, by which I am now so powerful and so majestic:
namely, generosity, self-control, and restraint.
Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana approached the Great Gabled Hall; having approached, he stood at the door of the Great Gabled Hall and uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Stop, sensual thought! Stop, thought of ill will! Stop, thought of cruelty!
This much, sensual thought; this much, thought of ill will; this much, thought of cruelty.
Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana entered the Great Gabled Hall made of gold.
Seated cross-legged, secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states,
he entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration.

With the fading away of rapture, he dwelt in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; he experienced happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness," and so he entered and dwelt in the third jhāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, having emerged from the great gabled chamber and entered the golden gabled chamber, sat upon a silver couch and dwelt pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness.

Likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwelt pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness.
He dwelt having suffused with his mind—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind accompanied by compassion...

He dwelt having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity. Likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.

There were eighty-four thousand gabled halls, headed by the Great Array Gabled Hall;
there were eighty-four thousand couches made of gold, silver, ivory, and sandalwood, covered with woolen rugs,

8. Attaining the Brahma World.
Then, Ānanda, not long after, King Mahāsudassana passed away.

Just as, Ānanda, a householder or a householder’s son, having eaten a delicious meal, experiences a drowsiness from the food, even so, Ānanda, was the death-agony sensation experienced by King Mahāsudassana.
And when King Mahāsudassana passed away, Ānanda, he was reborn in a happy destination, in the Brahmā world.
Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana spent eighty-four thousand years in princely play;
for eighty-four thousand years he exercised the office of viceroy.
He reigned for eighty-four thousand years.
For eighty-four thousand years, while remaining a householder, he lived the holy life in the Palace of Dhamma.
Having cultivated the four divine abodes, at the breaking up of the body after death, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Now, Ānanda, it might occur to you:
‘Perhaps at that time King Mahāsudassana was someone else.
But, Ānanda, it should not be viewed in this way. At that time, I was King Mahāsudassana.
To me belonged those eighty-four thousand cities, headed by the royal capital Kusāvatī;

to me belonged those eighty-four thousand palaces, headed by the Palace of Dharma (Dhammapāsāda); to me belonged those eighty-four thousand gabled chambers, headed by the Great Arrayed Gabled Chamber (Mahāviyūhakūṭāgāra);
to me belonged those eighty-four thousand couches made of gold, silver, ivory, and precious wood.

There were eighty-four thousand elephant-kings, headed by the royal elephant Uposatha, covered with blankets of fine cloth, spread with rugs of the finest kadalimiga deer-skin, provided with upper coverlets, and equipped with crimson foot-rugs at both ends;
they were adorned with golden ornaments, bearing golden banners, and draped in nets of gold. There were also eighty-four thousand horses.

Those eighty-four thousand chariots of mine, headed by the royal steed Valāhaka, were adorned with golden ornaments, bearing golden banners, covered with nets of gold, and draped with lion skins, tiger skins, leopard skins, and pale woolen blankets; likewise, those eighty-four thousand chariots,
headed by the Vejayanta chariot, were adorned with golden ornaments, bearing golden banners, and covered with nets of gold.
Those eighty-four thousand jewels of mine, headed by the jewel-treasure; those eighty-four thousand women of mine, headed by Queen Subhaddā;
those eighty-four thousand householders of mine, headed by the householder-treasure;
those eighty-four thousand kṣatriyas of mine, my followers, headed by the counselor-treasure; [all] mine.
Those eighty-four thousand milch cows had milk-pails for their stalls and bronze vessels as their receptacles;
those eighty-four thousand millions of garments of mine consisted of fine linen, fine cotton, fine silk, and fine wool;
those eighty-four thousand servings of boiled rice were brought to me as a meal-offering morning and evening.
"Moreover, Ānanda, among those eighty-four thousand cities, there was only one city in which I dwelt at that time, namely the royal capital Kusāvatī.
Among those eighty-four thousand palaces, there was only one palace in which I dwelt at that time, namely the Dhamma Palace.
Among those eighty-four thousand gabled chambers, there was only one gabled chamber in which I dwelt at that time, namely the Great Arrayed Gabled Chamber."
Moreover, Ānanda, of those eighty-four thousand couches, there was only one couch that I used at that time, namely one made of gold, or silver, or ivory, or sandalwood.
Furthermore, Ānanda, of those eighty-four thousand elephants, there was only one elephant that I rode at that time, namely the royal elephant Uposatha.
"Furthermore, Ānanda, among those eighty-four thousand horses, there was only one horse that I rode at that time, namely the horse-king Valāhaka.
Among those eighty-four thousand chariots, there was only one chariot that I rode at that time, namely the Vejayanta chariot.
Among those eighty-four thousand women, there was only one woman who attended upon me at that time, whether she was of the Khattiya caste or the Vessa caste."
Moreover, Ānanda, among those eighty-four thousand million garments,
there was only that single pair of robes which at that time I wore— whether it was fine linen, or fine cotton,
or fine silk, or fine wool.
"Moreover, Ānanda, of those eighty-four thousand dishes of rice, there was only one single dish of rice from which I ate at most a handful of boiled rice along with a suitable curry.
Behold, Ānanda, all these conditioned phenomena are past, ceased, and changed.
Thus, Ānanda, are conditioned phenomena impermanent."
Thus indeed, Ānanda, conditioned phenomena are unstable;
thus indeed, Ānanda, conditioned phenomena are not a source of comfort.
To this extent, Ānanda, it is sufficient to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, sufficient to become dispassionate toward them, and sufficient to be liberated from them.
Moreover, Ānanda, I recall having had my body laid down in this very place on six occasions;
and that was when I was a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of Dharma, conqueror of the four quarters,
who had established stability in the land and was possessed of the seven treasures— this was the seventh laying down of the body.

“Furthermore, Ānanda, I do not perceive any place in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, where the Tathāgata might lay down his eighth body.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further spoke as follows:
“Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena,
subject to arising and passing away;
having arisen, they cease.”
The subsiding of these is bliss.
The Mahāsudassana Sutta is finished; it is the fourth.
